articles.title: Gen Z turns to crypto as gateway to investing, WazirX data shows
articles.text:
Gen Z turns to crypto as gateway to investing, WazirX data shows
India’s Gen Z is entering financial markets earlier, with crypto emerging as a gateway to investing. WazirX data shows young investors favour diversified portfolios and are increasingly coming from Tier II and Tier III cities.
India's Gen Z is entering financial markets earlier and increasingly using cryptocurrency as a gateway to investing, while showing a preference for diversified portfolios and a willingness to stay invested through market volatility, data from crypto exchange WazirX showed.
Nearly 44.4% of Gen Z investors on the platform began their investment journey through crypto, suggesting that a large share of young investors are entering financial markets through digital assets rather than adding crypto to established portfolios.
The median age of Gen Z investors on WazirX is 25, while the generation accounted for 72% of all new investors on the platform in the first half of 2026. Gen Z also made up 32.1% of active traders, the company said.
The trend is spreading beyond India's largest cities. Nearly 80% of WazirX's Gen Z users come from outside the country's top 10 cities, highlighting the growing participation of investors from Tier II and Tier III centres. Mumbai and Delhi continue to have the highest individual concentration of users.
The data also challenges the perception that young crypto investors are primarily chasing speculative assets. Gen Z users allocate 25% of their portfolios to established "blue-chip" cryptocurrencies, 16% to memecoins and 59% to utility-focused categories including decentralised finance, Layer-2 ecosystems and payment tokens.
The figures indicate that while memecoins remain part of the investment mix, the majority of Gen Z holdings are concentrated in categories WazirX associates with utility, liquidity and longer-term potential.
Young investors are also showing a willingness to buy during market downturns rather than retreating from crypto, according to WazirX.
About 52.8% of Gen Z investors buy during mild market corrections, while 43.7% continue buying even on the worst trading days. Their average investment size remains nearly unchanged during major market declines compared with normal trading days, the exchange said.
The data suggests that some young investors are increasingly treating market corrections as opportunities to accumulate assets, while using rallies to rebalance portfolios or realise gains.
WazirX's findings come as its broader user base also becomes increasingly concentrated outside India's major metropolitan areas. In a July report, the exchange said more than 82% of its users came from non-metro cities.
The Gen Z investor base on WazirX is also dominated by relatively young and lower-income participants. Nearly 79.6% have annual incomes between Rs 1 lakh and Rs 5 lakh.
Students account for 40% of Gen Z users, followed by salaried professionals at 33% and self-employed users at 27%, according to the company.
The findings suggest that crypto is being incorporated into investment strategies relatively early in the financial lives of many young Indians, rather than being used solely by investors who have already accumulated substantial wealth.
"Gen Z is proving that wealth creation isn't about where you come from or how much you start with, but finding the right opportunities, doing your research, and starting early. Young Indians were investing in crypto earlier, but they're doing so with discipline, curiosity, and a long-term mindset now. That's the foundation of India's next financial revolution," WazirX founder Nischal Shetty said.
The findings were released around International Youth Day, observed annually on August 12, which this year focuses attention on the role and aspirations of young people globally.
The data points to a growing role for digital assets in India's expanding retail-investor ecosystem, with Gen Z emerging as a significant new participant group and increasingly coming from outside the country's traditional financial centres.

articles.title: Ergonomic Hacks for Sedentary Tech Workers - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Tech work keeps software developers and system engineers attached to desk stations for 8 to 12 hours a day. Long desk sessions slowly take a toll on physical health, leading to tight joints and sluggish energy levels.
Small workplace upgrades create dramatic shifts in daily comfort and focus. Adopting smart ergonomic habits keeps your body resilient without sacrificing daily coding productivity.
Optimizing Monitor Placement for Neck Comfort
Staring down at a low screen causes severe strain on upper back muscles during long work hours. Positioning your monitor at eye level prevents neck strain and maintains optimal spinal alignment throughout long working hours. Correct height alignment stops developers from slumping forward during long coding sprints.
Keep the display about an arm’s length away to protect against severe eye fatigue. Adjusting screen brightness to match ambient room lighting keeps your vision sharp throughout the day. Simple monitor arms permit quick height adjustments across different work tasks.
Dual monitors require extra attention to prevent constant neck twisting throughout long shifts. Center the primary monitor directly in front of your main keyboard setup. Place secondary displays off to the side at identical height angles for smooth viewing.
Upgrading Desk Setup and Leg Support
Sitting in standard office chairs for extended periods restricts blood flow down to lower extremities. Many tech professionals rely on options such as compression stockings Australia to keep lower limb circulation steady throughout long workdays. Quality gear prevents fluid buildup and maintains leg comfort during marathon programming sessions.
Footrests offer targeted relief by supporting proper knee and hip alignment. Elevating your feet slightly reduces lower back pressure and keeps thighs parallel to the ground. Adjusting desk height permits your shoulders to relax completely.
Clear physical clutter from beneath your primary desk area. Ample legroom permits frequent position shifts throughout long work shifts. Freeing up leg space encourages natural stretching between coding tasks.
Selecting Supportive Chairs for Spinal Health
Quality office seating plays a foundational role in maintaining spine health over long desk shifts. Proper lumbar support maintains the natural inward curve of the lower spine. Adjustable backrests distribute body weight evenly across the entire chair base.
Adjustable armrests keep wrists level with your keyboard surface. Ergonomic seating features include:
- Seat depth controls to protect knee circulation
- Dynamic lumbar adjustments for spine support
- Pneumatic height controls for custom alignment
- Adjustable tilt tension to balance upper body support.
Proper armrest height stops shoulder tension from building up during deep work sessions.
Mesh chair backing promotes airflow to keep you cool during intense work hours. Cushioned seat pans prevent uncomfortable pressure points around hip joints. Reclining slightly backward reduces spinal disc compression during long code review sessions.
Managing Digital Eye Strain and Lighting
Screen glare forces eye muscles to work double time during dark evening shifts. Shift your workspace relative to windows to minimize harsh background reflections. Soft ambient room light reduces sharp contrast between monitors and surrounding walls.
Taking periodic breaks from monitor screens helps maintain visual comfort. Resting your eyes every 20 minutes keeps focusing muscles relaxed. Periodic blinking maintains surface hydration and protects eye comfort.
Font sizes on code editors need generous scaling for physical comfort. Enlarging code text prevents leaning forward toward high-resolution screens. Dark mode themes lower glare when coding late into the night.
Modern tech careers require proactive habits to safeguard physical health. Simple adjustments to workspace tools make daily desk routines far more comfortable.
Consistent attention to posture and movement builds lasting energy. Small daily changes preserve your physical well-being throughout long programming sessions.

articles.title: Ahora que España entera ha alucinado con el eclipse, la buena noticia: el mapa del eclipse total del año que viene
articles.text:
Ayer, a las 20:26, media España estaba mirando al oeste con unas gafas de cartón puestas; a las 20:45 estaba escribiendo "increíble" en Instagram y hoy, mientras procesan lo que vieron ayer por la tarde, ya están escribiendo "siguiente eclipse" en su buscador de confianza. Lo sabemos porque, en fin, nosotros hemos hecho exactamente lo mismo.
Y la pregunta tiene dos respuestas: una buena y una mala. La buena es que el siguiente eclipse total de sol que tocará territorio español es en menos de un año, el 2 de agosto de 2027. Es más, quitando lo melancólico del atardecer eclipsado, será mejor en casi todo.
La mala noticia es que si el de 2026 ya fue problemático a nivel de movimiento, el de 2027 va a convertirse rápidamente en una pesadilla logística. Por eso hemos hecho un mapa. Si queremos verlo bien, hay que ponerse las pilas ya.
¿Cómo que será "mejor en casi todo"? Es cierto que la imagen de un sol ocultándose aún medio eclipsado es difícil de superar. Los colores y el ambiente que se pudieron ver este año son difícilmente emulables. El precio de esa imagen fue que el horizonte se convirtió en el gran problema a la hora de verlo.
Como el sol estaba casi apoyado en la línea, cualquier colina, edificio o nubes podían fastidiarnos la vista. En 2027, el eclipse ocurrirá a media mañana. Y eso significa que sí, las nubes pueden empañarnos la vista, pero si estás en la zona de totalidad da igual el pueblo, la orientación y el balcón: el eclipse ocurrirá arriba, el mundo se oscurecerá en mitad de la mañana.
Además, durará más del doble (y casi el triple en las mejores zonas). El máximo ayer fue de un minuto y 50 segundos en una pequeña zona de Asturias. En Ceuta el de 2027 durará 4 minutos y 48 segundos. En Cádiz capital durará 2 minutos y 54 segundos.
¿Y dónde se podrá ver? Los municipios españoles dentro de la zona de totalidad son menos que los de este año: poco más de un centenar de municipios del extremo sur. Y aquí empiezan los problemas.
Si, como digo, el eclipse de ayer era técnicamente difícil de ver con su sol bajo, su horizonte problemático y su minuto escaso; el de 2027 será una pesadilla logística. Hablamos del primer lunes de agosto en la costa más llena de España durante la semana más llena del año. Y, por si fuera poco, ahora sí que toda Europa está avisada tras las imágenes de 2026.
No hay duda de que, al ser a media mañana, habrá gente que podrá salir de Madrid de madrugada, verlo y volverse a su casa. Pero esa posibilidad, solo suma más presión a zona que tendrá un montón de problemas de tráfico, ocupación y sobrecarga de infraestructuras.
Más allá de España. Por supuesto, el mapa solo se centra en los datos del eclipse en España. Se podrá ver también en buena parte del norte de África y, de hecho, en Luxor (Egipto) durará unos seis minutos, que es lo más cerca del máximo que vamos a ver en las próximas décadas. Es algo, todo sea dicho, que de verdad que nadie podrá volver a ver nunca.
Así que sí, si queremos verlo bien, es momento de ponerse a planificar.

articles.title: Samsung Odyssey G80HS 32" Review: Going 6K
articles.text:
The Samsung Odyssey G80HS is the first 6K gaming monitor, which immediately raises an obvious question: who exactly needs a 6K gaming monitor? It's a crazy resolution for gaming and far too demanding to make much sense with today's GPUs at native resolution. But the G80HS has a few tricks designed to make that seemingly excessive spec more practical.
Its 6K mode is primarily aimed at high-DPI productivity. You get a large 32-inch IPS LCD panel with no risk of burn-in and a 165Hz refresh rate that keeps desktop use feeling smooth and responsive. None of the sluggish 60Hz experience that has plagued high-DPI monitors for far too long.
Then, for gaming, Samsung offers a 3K dual mode that drops the resolution to something much more manageable for today's GPUs while doubling the refresh rate to 330Hz. Variable refresh rates are supported, Samsung claims fast response times, and the overall package is meant to deliver a genuine high-end gaming experience.
What's the catch? The Odyssey G80HS costs $1,600, which is very expensive.
That's about double the price of a 32-inch 4K 240Hz OLED monitor. It also has, uh... questionable HDR performance, which we'll get into later. No spoilers just yet.
But while it is expensive for a gaming monitor, it's not crazy for a high-DPI productivity display. Asus, for example, sells the 32-inch 6K ProArt PA32QCV for $1,300, but that model is limited to 60Hz. For me, and probably plenty of others considering a display like this, that's a non-starter.
The 6K Resolution
The Odyssey G80HS's biggest selling point is its 6144 x 3456 resolution. This is an exceptionally sharp monitor capable of producing excellent levels of detail. At a 32-inch panel size, that resolution results in a pixel density of 220 PPI, nearly 60% higher than a standard 4K screen. Up against the 32-inch 4K LCDs and OLEDs that I use daily, I felt the improvement from 6K was immediately noticeable.
This 32-inch 6K panel has a similar pixel density to a 27-inch 5K panel, with both forming part of a new wave of high-DPI, gaming-class displays. These screens make more sense when viewed around a target pixel density rather than a specific resolution. The 32-inch model is larger and provides more screen real estate than a 27-inch display, so pushing the resolution from 5K to 6K maintains that same high-density experience while giving you more pixels to work with.
The biggest benefits of 6K come from desktop productivity. Text quality is outstanding, with noticeably sharper edges than on 4K screens, while high-resolution photos can be displayed with greater detail.
The end result is similar to 27-inch 5K because the pixel density is essentially the same, but the jump from 4K to 6K at 32 inches is more substantial than going from 4K to 5K at 27 inches. That's simply because the increase in pixel density is larger. It's a big win for people that love a large panel but also love a high-DPI experience.
Another productivity advantage is the increased pixel real estate, especially when working with high-resolution assets. If you're editing a 4K image in Photoshop, for example, a 4K monitor can't display that image at 100% scale while also leaving room for the application interface. You typically need to reduce the image to around 66% to fit everything on screen.
On a 6K display, you can view the same 4K image at full resolution and 100% scale while still leaving roughly 60% of the screen available for Photoshop's interface and tools. Viewing the image at 100% is preferable because you're seeing the source without scaling artifacts. For workloads like this, 6K is genuinely a much better experience.
For gaming, the benefits are less significant. We tried a range of games at the full 6K resolution and, don't get me wrong, they looked absolutely brilliant in terms of detail and sharpness. It's clearly an improvement over 4K, but not a transformative one. A 32-inch 4K display already looks very sharp for gaming.
The problem is the extreme performance cost. A 6144 x 3456 image contains 2.5x as many pixels as 4K, so your GPU has dramatically more work to do for what is ultimately nowhere near a 2.5x improvement in visual quality. Getting much above 60 FPS at 6K is difficult even with high-end GPUs.
For example, we hooked the monitor up to a GeForce RTX 5080, and to consistently stay above 60 FPS in Cyberpunk 2077 at 6K, we had to use the High preset with ray tracing disabled and DLSS set to Performance mode. The same configuration at 4K delivered over 110 FPS, making much better use of a high-refresh-rate display.
The new Lego Batman game provided another good example. It looks gorgeous at 6K thanks to its excellent texture quality, but reaching 60 FPS required dropping the preset to Medium and again using DLSS Performance upscaling.
With current hardware, this simply isn't a monitor where you can expect to combine its maximum resolution with maximum graphics settings in demanding games.
That's specifically true of modern triple-A gaming, though. There are plenty of games where the extra resolution is useful and the performance penalty matters much less. Titles heavy on interfaces and fine details, such as strategy games and city builders, look fantastic at 6K. Lightweight 2D games and many indie titles are also particularly well suited to the resolution.
Dual Mode: 3K at 330Hz
While 6K may not be ideal for gaming overall, the G80HS has a neat trick up its sleeve: Dual Mode functionality. Dual Mode allows the monitor to run at a lower resolution, typically one-quarter of native, while increasing the refresh rate, usually to double the native maximum. Because the panel starts at 6K, the trade-off is much more appealing here than on most other dual-mode displays.
On 4K dual-mode monitors, the lower-resolution configuration is typically 1080p, which is a substantial downgrade in sharpness, especially on a 32-inch panel. I certainly don't want to play most games at 1080p on a display this large.
But on a 6K monitor like the G80HS, Dual Mode drops to 3072 x 1728, or 3K, while the refresh rate increases from 165Hz to 330Hz. A 3K resolution on a 32-inch panel is far more usable and works well across a wide range of games without the major loss in visual quality we saw with 1080p dual modes.
As with other monitors, Dual Mode works seamlessly here. Enable the option in the OSD, and the resolution drops while the refresh rate increases. There are no other meaningful compromises: color performance, contrast, and input lag are preserved just as they are in the 6K mode.
Samsung has also mapped Dual Mode to a right press of the OSD toggle for quick access, although strangely it isn't a simple on/off switch. It also cycles through the 24-inch emulation mode, which is a little annoying when you just want to quickly disable Dual Mode.
The G80HS does not use strict integer scaling in its 3K Dual Mode. A single 3K pixel is typically represented by four primary native pixels, with up to four additional pixels activated at lower brightness. This gets closer to a native-like presentation than most other dual-mode monitors, so I think it looks quite good. It's also worth remembering that a native 6K panel can never look exactly like a native 3K panel because of inherent differences in subpixel layout at the hardware level.
Subpixel Layouts
The 3K mode is obviously not as sharp or detailed as native 6K, and the downgrade can feel substantial if you've been using the 6K mode for a while. Text and desktop apps are blurrier, and you lose the crystal-clear sharpness of the native resolution.
Broadly speaking, though, it looks similar to a 27-inch 1440p panel, perhaps slightly softer, and that's still a very usable level of clarity. It's nowhere near the downgrade we saw on 4K dual-mode monitors running at 1080p, where the image can look very blurry on a 32-inch screen. By comparison, 3K Dual Mode looks quite reasonable.
You wouldn't use the 3K mode in situations where that loss of resolution is especially noticeable. For text-heavy desktop applications, we'd simply leave the monitor at 6K. The real advantage is gaming, where 3K provides what is, at worst, roughly a 1440p-like experience.
I was very satisfied with the level of detail and clarity in this mode. In-game interfaces still look good in most cases, the image doesn't appear overly blurry, and overall it's an excellent resolution for gaming. After about 10 minutes of gameplay, you quickly stop thinking about the fact that you're not getting the full native 6K experience.
Gaming at 3K is also far less demanding than 6K, so you're trading some top-end clarity and sharpness for more than double the frame rate at the same settings. In my opinion, that's a much better balance. The 3K Dual Mode works well across essentially all types of games and is my preferred way to play most titles on this monitor.
That makes the G80HS an unusually versatile display. The native 6K mode delivers excellent text clarity and elite sharpness for desktop applications and productivity, while the 3K 330Hz mode is much better suited to high-performance gaming, avoiding the enormous performance hit of running games at 6K while also doubling the maximum refresh rate.
Neither mode feels overly compromised. You're getting much closer to the best of both worlds, and this is one of the first implementations where Dual Mode genuinely lives up to its promise.
Response Time Performance
The Odyssey G80HS does offer adjustable overdrive settings, but only when adaptive sync is disabled. Most people are going to use this display with G-Sync, FreeSync, or some form of VRR enabled, in which case the overdrive settings are grayed out and Samsung's default tuning is used. So that's what we'll focus on here: response time performance with VRR enabled.
Starting with the 6K configuration at the maximum 165Hz refresh rate, performance is decent, with an average response time of 7.42ms and no noticeable overshoot artifacts. This isn't quite as fast as we'd like to see at 165Hz, but it gets reasonably close, and cumulative deviation is good. Essentially, the gaming experience at 6K 165Hz is solid enough, assuming you can actually run games at that sort of frame rate.
As the refresh rate decreases in the 6K mode, performance hovers around an 8ms response time average, with no overshoot all the way down to 60Hz.
Cumulative deviation remains good, while refresh compliance indicates reasonable support for at least 120Hz, if not a little higher. Ideally, performance would be slightly faster, but given that most games at 6K will probably run toward the lower end of the refresh range, it's good to see response times hold up there. The result is effectively a single overdrive mode experience across the refresh range.
Compared with other displays at their maximum refresh rates, the G80HS isn't especially fast, but it's also not drastically outside the range we typically see from IPS LCDs.
The 5K LG 27GM950B is slightly faster in terms of raw response times, but in cumulative deviation, the 5K and 6K options are essentially neck and neck. It's also good to confirm that the G80HS doesn't suffer from the sort of speed issues we saw with displays like the BenQ EX321UX or LG 27G850A. A cumulative deviation result of around 500 is only about 20% behind the Gigabyte M32UP near the top of the chart, so overall we're seeing fairly typical Fast IPS performance.
Across the refresh rate range, Samsung has optimized the panel to minimize overshoot artifacts, which is why its average response time results sit toward the lower end of the chart. But cumulative deviation, which accounts for the balance between response speed and overshoot, places the G80HS firmly in the middle of the pack for an IPS LCD. It offers an almost identical experience to the 27GM950B and most other high-resolution LCDs.
The major difference comes when comparing it with OLED. OLED panels are an order of magnitude faster in response times and therefore offer much better motion clarity at the same refresh rate. The 240Hz PG32UCDM3 at the top of the chart is roughly twice as clear in fast motion as the G80HS at 165Hz.
The G80HS isn't particularly fast at 120Hz or 60Hz either, but we're not seeing any problematic results such as excessive overshoot.
The 3K Dual Mode configuration uses different response time tuning from the 6K mode, allowing the panel to run a little faster at the same refresh rate. At 165Hz, for example, the average response time improves from 7.4ms at 6K to 5.7ms at 3K.
This more aggressive tuning is largely necessary to push the display toward its 330Hz maximum. Even so, the panel isn't fast enough to deliver a true 330Hz response time experience. At 330Hz, transitions need to complete within roughly 3ms to keep pace with each refresh, and the G80HS falls well short of that target. As a result, we run into refresh compliance issues where some pixel transitions take longer to complete than the refresh cycle itself.
This only resolves at around the 200Hz mark, meaning refresh rates above that are bottlenecked to some degree by the panel's response times. On the positive side, there isn't much overshoot at those higher refresh rates.
Through the middle and lower portions of the refresh range, the 3K mode averages around 6ms, although overshoot becomes increasingly noticeable as the refresh rate drops. At 60Hz, performance improves, but this doesn't appear to be the result of variable overdrive. Instead, at around 62Hz the monitor typically switches to a double-rate configuration. This means a 60Hz VRR input is actually displayed with the panel refreshing at 120Hz, despite the monitor reporting a minimum VRR refresh rate of 48Hz.
Between 120Hz and just above 60Hz, the inverse ghosting rate sits at around 30 to 40%, producing noticeable artifact trails behind moving objects. It isn't a complete deal breaker, but this part of the refresh range could have been better optimized. In practice, the 3K mode works best between roughly 140 and 220Hz, where the panel is fast enough while keeping artifacts to a minimum.
At its maximum 330Hz refresh rate, the G80HS is ultimately unimpressive compared with other high-refresh-rate monitors. Performance is somewhat better in Dual Mode overall, and the 330Hz configuration is certainly usable, but it doesn't match what you'd get from a dedicated 1440p 330Hz gaming monitor using a faster IPS LCD panel.
Input lag is low in both the 6K and 3K modes, with processing delay below 1ms. That's standard for a modern gaming monitor and allows for a responsive experience. For the lowest latency and best overall responsiveness, you'll want to use the display in its 330Hz mode, although the 6K mode still feels smooth and is far more responsive than a typical 60Hz display.
SDR Color Performance
Color Space: Samsung Odyssey G80HS - D65-P3
The Odyssey G80HS is a wide-gamut monitor, though its gamut isn't especially wide by modern standards. We're looking at 94% coverage of DCI-P3, which falls a little short of the full coverage we'd ideally like to see in 2026, while Rec. 2020 coverage reaches 74%. This puts the G80HS within the normal range for IPS LCDs, but behind the latest QD-OLED displays and LG's 5K monitor, which has an exceptionally wide gamut.
Default Color Performance
Factory calibration is okay. Gamma performance is good, particularly if you're after a flat 2.2 response, though my unit had a slight blue tint out of the box, resulting in a color temperature of around 7,000K. There's also some oversaturation by default due to the wide-gamut nature of the display, which expands SDR Rec. 709 colors to fill the monitor's native gamut.
Default ACM Color Performance
There are a couple of ways to improve the SDR experience. One is to use Windows 11's Auto Color Management. This doesn't change grayscale performance, but it does reduce oversaturation and properly maps sRGB colors, resulting in a ColorChecker deltaE average of 6.8. That's still only an average result, but it's an improvement over the default configuration.
sRGB Mode Color Performance
You can also switch the G80HS into its sRGB mode by changing the color space setting. Importantly, this still allows adjustment of the other monitor settings, including white balance. Again, this mode doesn't change much in terms of grayscale performance, and color performance is slightly worse than with Auto Color Management, but it's a useful option for devices or operating systems that don't support color management.
Grayscale performance in the sRGB mode isn't particularly impressive compared with other monitors. We're typically looking for a deltaE average below 5.0, and the G80HS falls short of that target, placing it toward the bottom of the chart. ColorChecker performance isn't great either. We wouldn't describe it as terrible, but comparatively, it's not at the level of many other 32-inch options.
The saving grace is that Samsung provides plenty of color controls, allowing you to make meaningful improvements through the monitor's hardware settings. We were able to reduce the grayscale deltaE to 3.0, correct the white balance, and improve the ColorChecker deltaE to 4.2. Those are strong results that we'd consider well calibrated. Our optimal settings are available to Patreon members.
OSD Tweaked Color Performance
Calibrated Color Performance
Further calibration can clean up the remaining inaccuracies, with a full Calman calibration producing excellent results. So while the G80HS doesn't offer particularly strong calibration out of the box, certainly not at the level we'd expect from a professional-grade monitor, that makes some sense given this is primarily a gaming display. With some adjustment, it can perform very well for SDR work and even some DCI-P3 content creation, provided you're comfortable with the panel not covering the entire P3 gamut.
Brightness, Contrast, Uniformity
Maximum brightness is sufficient at 445 nits, putting the G80HS right within the normal range for modern IPS LCDs. It doesn't do anything particularly special here, and monitors with proper mini-LED backlights can get much brighter, with LG's 5K model reaching around 800 nits. But for standard indoor use, around 450 nits is more than enough in my opinion. Minimum brightness of 63 nits is below average, but isn't anything crazy bad.
The native contrast ratio is pretty good for an IPS LCD. I recorded a result of 1,940:1 after calibration, putting it in the ballpark of LG's IPS Black panels, even though I don't believe the G80HS uses an IPS Black panel.
It's obviously still well short of VA LCDs and OLEDs, and black level performance remains relatively poor overall. Still, I was pleasantly surprised to see better-than-average IPS contrast, which helps mitigate one of the technology's main weaknesses.
Viewing angles are fine, ranging from good to slightly below average compared with other IPS LCDs. The bigger problem for LCDs these days is competition from OLEDs, which offer substantially better viewing angles with less brightness shift when viewed off-axis. For most people, the G80HS should be fine, but its viewing angles aren't at the level of an OLED.
Panel uniformity also falls short of OLED. QD-OLED panels are generally very uniform from edge to edge, so if that's a priority, a 32-inch 4K QD-OLED will be the better choice. I'd describe uniformity on the G80HS as mediocre.
My unit was somewhat patchy, with noticeable brightness falloff along the left and right edges compared with the center. This isn't particularly obvious in many situations, but if you're considering this 6K monitor primarily for productivity, it could become annoying in applications with large, uniform backgrounds.
Design, Features, Ports
The G80HS's built-in features are accessed through the OSD, controlled by a directional toggle in a slightly awkward location on the rear of the monitor. Unfortunately, the toggle itself feels terrible to use. Pressing it inward to select an option sometimes feels like I'm flexing the PCB it's attached to, and the entire mechanism comes across as surprisingly cheap.
The feature set itself is decent. There are plenty of color controls for fine-tuning white balance, gamma, shadow detail, and other aspects of the image. Local dimming can be disabled, which we'd recommend, and Samsung includes several gaming features such as a black equalizer and crosshairs. However, there's no picture-in-picture mode, KVM switch, or black frame insertion. Firmware updates are supported over USB.
Port selection consists of one DisplayPort 2.1 UHBR13.5 connection, two full-bandwidth HDMI 2.1 48 Gbps ports, and a two-port USB 5 Gbps hub. There's no USB-C input.
Both DisplayPort and HDMI require DSC to run the monitor at 6K 165Hz. That would still be the case even if Samsung had used DisplayPort 2.1 UHBR20, as the bandwidth required exceeds 80 Gbps. Our guess is that Samsung opted for UHBR13.5 to simplify the hardware design, and in practice it has no meaningful impact on the product.
One important limitation is that a DisplayPort 1.4 connection only allows the monitor to run at 6K 60Hz. DisplayPort 2.1 is required for higher refresh rates over DP. This means GPUs limited to DisplayPort 1.4, such as the GeForce RTX 40 series, need to use HDMI 2.1 instead to access the monitor's maximum refresh rate.
The overall design of the G80HS isn't that impressive in my opinion, especially considering its $1,600 price. That's firmly high-end territory, yet the build quality and choice of materials feel more in line with some of the budget monitors I've tested. The stand base, for example, is covered in fairly basic black plastic, while competing high-end displays increasingly use thinner and more premium metal bases.
From the front, the design is dominated by the 32-inch panel, with slim bezels on three sides and a small chin along the bottom edge. It looks fine, and Samsung uses a standard matte coating similar to what we've seen on other IPS LCDs, which I think is appropriate for this type of monitor.
The rear is again dominated by fairly basic black plastic. The monitor itself is relatively thin, which is nice to see for an LCD, but the materials leave something to be desired and I wouldn't describe the overall design as especially sleek. There's also an RGB LED ring surrounding the stand connection, which looks fine enough.
The stand supports height, tilt, and swivel adjustment, with a good range of height adjustment available. Its base is also flat, making it easy to place small items on top, which is a nice practical bonus.
A Great 6K Monitor With One Big Weakness
Overall, the Samsung Odyssey G80HS is a very interesting monitor, and unique in being the first 6K display that's genuinely suitable for gaming. There are really two questions to answer with this one: is the G80HS a good monitor, and is it a good value?
On the first point, we think Samsung has largely succeeded in what it set out to achieve. The 6K resolution looks brilliant, delivering excellent text clarity and tons of pixel real estate, making this a great high-DPI display for productivity work.
The 165Hz refresh rate in the 6K mode is also a massive improvement over previous 6K 60Hz panels, making desktop use much smoother than on many professional monitors. Personally, 60Hz is an absolute deal breaker for me, so getting a high-density screen with a genuinely good refresh rate is a major step forward.
The G80HS has strong gaming chops as well. Native 6K is obviously challenging to run in demanding titles, although lightweight games look fantastic at such a high resolution. But it's really the 3K Dual Mode that makes this a viable gaming monitor.
At 3072 x 1728, it's much less demanding, still looks good in my opinion with similar sharpness to a 27-inch 1440p display, and comes with a 330Hz maximum refresh rate.
This panel actually delivers on the promise of Dual Mode, unlike older 4K models with a crappy, low-resolution 1080p mode that was really only suitable for certain competitive games. On the G80HS, I'd recommend the 3K configuration for most games, and I thought it worked really well.
The combination of these two modes gives the G80HS an unusually broad range of capabilities. You get a super-sharp 6K mode for productivity and a faster 3K mode for gaming, all within the same 32-inch panel. Neither mode feels like a major compromise, and that versatility is probably the monitor's greatest strength.
Response time performance is good enough. This isn't a slow monitor, but it isn't particularly fast either, and the 3K configuration could have been tuned better, especially considering Samsung locks the overdrive controls when VRR is enabled. OLEDs are, of course, much faster than this IPS LCD, and if motion clarity is your top priority, you should probably choose an OLED instead. On the whole, though, the G80HS is fast enough for gaming without problematic blur trails or other major response time issues.
Factory calibration is more disappointing. We suspect plenty of buyers interested in a 6K display will be using it for productivity and potentially some content creation.
While this isn't a professional display, as it's part of Samsung's Odyssey gaming line, we would have liked to see better out-of-the-box calibration for creators. It can be manually calibrated to perform very well, but given that it's priced in the same territory as professional-grade 6K displays, albeit 60Hz models, some extra attention here would have been appreciated.
The biggest omission is proper HDR hardware, which is highly disappointing given the $1,600 price. At this price point in 2026, we think it's reasonable to expect a proper mini-LED local dimming backlight, but the G80HS instead uses a crappy edge-lit local dimming system with what appears to be around eight zones. Peak brightness also tops out at around 440 nits, well short of what we'd want for a compelling HDR experience.
There's really no way around it: this monitor looks bad with HDR content, especially compared with cheaper displays that offer proper HDR hardware, such as 32-inch OLEDs and some 4K mini-LED LCDs. Black levels are frequently raised, brightness is limited, and the panel simply can't produce the contrast required to show HDR content as intended.
Despite the poor HDR experience, we still think the G80HS is a good product for 6K productivity work with SDR gaming on the side. If you're aware of that limitation and primarily want it for the high-DPI experience, it's something we could recommend.
The Price is the Bigger Problem
Whether it's good value is much more complicated. Professional 32-inch 6K 60Hz monitors are available for around $1,300 these days, so Samsung is effectively offering a much higher refresh rate plus a proper gaming mode for about 20% more.
It doesn't provide the professional-grade calibration we'd expect from something like the Asus ProArt alternative, but given the refresh rate and gaming capabilities, we'd say it's at least somewhat competitive within the 6K segment. It's expensive, but not completely outrageous relative to other displays at the same resolution.
As a gaming monitor, however, the value proposition is much harder to justify. The G80HS is extremely expensive compared with the broader gaming monitor market, and the lack of true HDR significantly weakens the package.
You'd have to be absolutely certain you want the 6K resolution to seriously consider this product. Otherwise, it makes very little sense. That makes the G80HS a relatively niche display, and it's hard to imagine mainstream gamers choosing it at this price.
The biggest problem Samsung faces is that 32-inch 4K 240Hz OLEDs are substantially cheaper. Yes, they have a lower resolution, but they're faster, offer proper HDR, deliver much better contrast and uniformity, and 4K already strikes a good balance between image clarity and gaming performance.
Excellent 4K QD-OLEDs can be found for around $800, half the price of the G80HS, which makes the 6K option very difficult to recommend purely for gaming. I'd say the same applies even for productivity. I use a 4K QD-OLED for work every day, and given the enormous price difference, I'd personally buy one of those instead of the G80HS unless I specifically needed the additional pixel density.
The G80HS would become much more competitive at a more reasonable price, perhaps around $1,000 or slightly less. Samsung is known for heavily discounting its monitors, so it's entirely possible we'll see it closer to that level during sales later in its life. But at the launch MSRP, you really need to prioritize the 6K resolution and high-DPI experience over everything else to even consider the G80HS at that price.

This 4TB Team Group T-Force G50 SSD for $389.99, thanks to a $106 discount code at Newegg, isn't a record breaker, but it's basically the lowest price you'll pay for this amount of storage for an SSD offering Gen 4 speeds, and $10 cheaper than we saw during Prime Day.

Save on this M.2 2280 4Tb PCIe 4.0 SSD with promo code BTSF2997, which makes this the cheapest 4TB SSD on the market right now, give or take a few cents.

Don't forget to use coupon code BTSF2997 for the discount, however.

articles.title: La nouvelle prime pour les voitures électriques d’occasion est particulièrement décevante
articles.text:
Il aura fallu attendre le 12 août 2026 pour voir publier au Journal officiel l’un des textes très attendus concernant les primes à l’achat de véhicules électriques d’occasion. L’arrêté du 10 août 2026 crée la fiche CEE « TRA-EQ-133 » : un nouveau dispositif qui promet sur le papier une aide pouvant atteindre jusqu’à plus de 2 000 €, mais qui est en réalité réservée à quelques cas très spécifiques.
Pour les acheteurs particuliers, il faudra se contenter d’un coup de pouce d’environ 330 €. Une somme relativement dérisoire qui résonne comme une mauvaise blague lorsqu’on la recontextualise.
Pour qui, comment, combien : ce qu’il faut retenir de cette prime occasion
Pour espérer bénéficier de l’aide de 337 € en moyenne (42,2 MWh cumac par véhicule : le montant varie sensiblement selon les certificats d’économie d’énergie), le texte officiel impose un cumul de critères stricts qui restreint considérablement le nombre d’acheteurs éligibles, ainsi que les véhicules ciblés :
- Achat chez un professionnel obligatoire : Le véhicule doit être acheté ou loué (LLD/LOA d’au moins 3 ans) par un pro. Les transactions entre particuliers, qui représentent pourtant le cœur du marché de l’occasion en France, sont totalement exclues.
- Contrôle de santé de la batterie : L’état de santé certifié de la batterie (SoH) doit être supérieur à 80 % (ou afficher une autonomie résiduelle d’au moins 200 km si le SoH ne peut être vérifié).
- Engagement de conservation : L’acheteur doit s’engager à conserver le véhicule au moins 3 ans, qu’il soit acheté ou loué.
- Véhicules éligibles : La voiture doit être 100 % électrique, immatriculée en France entre le 1er janvier 2017 et le 31 décembre 2023, peser moins de 1 800 kg et ne pas dépasser 25 000 € (ces deux derniers critères concernent uniquement la bonification des aides à domicile).
- Limite du nombre de véhicules : Chaque bénéficiaire est juridiquement limité à cinq véhicules.
- Durée du dispositif : Le dispositif démarre au 1er septembre 2026. Pour la bonification, l’opération doit en plus être engagée avant le 1er janvier 2027 et achevée avant le 1er juillet 2027.
L’occasion : toujours le parent pauvre de la transition énergétique
Depuis la suppression de l’ancien bonus occasion de 1 000 € en février 2024, l’État avait tout simplement abandonné le marché de l’occasion électrique. Après un peu plus de 3 ans d’existence, le gouvernement estimait que les véhicules électriques d’occasion, moins chers que les modèles neufs, nécessitaient moins de soutien public. La mesure répondait aussi à un objectif d’économie budgétaire, avec environ 25 millions d’euros d’économies attendues. Seules subsistaient alors quelques aides locales très disparates dans certaines régions.
Pendant ce temps, le gouvernement a continué à encourager l’achat de véhicules neufs, par le biais du bonus écologique (puis du coup de pouce CEE) et du leasing social, une solution censée permettre aux foyers modestes d’accéder au véhicule électrique (neuf).
Accorder 330 € environ pour une voiture de seconde main qui coûte en moyenne 15 000 € à 20 000 €, c’est à peine plus élevé que les primes accordées pour un vélo électrique ou un quadricycle sans permis. Par rapport à l’ancien bonus occasion de 1 000 €, ouvert aux particuliers pour une électrique d’occasion âgée d’au moins deux ans et conservée deux ans, la nouvelle aide CEE est plus ciblée et bien moins généreuse. Elle impose notamment un achat auprès d’un professionnel, une batterie affichant plus de 80 % de capacité et un engagement de conservation ou de location de trois ans.
Une bonification pour les professionnels des services à domicile
La nouvelle aide comporte trois niveaux : un forfait de base d’environ 337 €, puis une bonification multipliant le volume de CEE par quatre (soit environ 1 350 €) lorsque le véhicule est affecté à des prestations au bénéfice d’un ménage en précarité énergétique, et par six dans les autres cas éligibles pour les professionnels de l’aide à domicile, soit environ 2 000 à 2 360 €.
Difficile, en revanche, de comprendre à qui s’applique exactement le coefficient 4 et donc l’aide d’environ 1 350 € : les joies du langage administratif.
Le montant maximal est réservé à une bonification temporaire destinée aux services autonomie à domicile et aux professionnels de l’aide, de l’accompagnement et des services à la personne sans distinction de localisation. Pour ces professionnels qui accumulent les kilomètres, l’aide CEE peut effectivement monter jusqu’à 2 000 € (voire un peu plus selon le cours du kWh cumac), à condition de signer leur contrat avant la fin de l’année 2026.
Le contour de ce nouveau dispositif ne semble pas vraiment être le coup de pouce espéré ni pour les professionnels de l’aide à domicile ni pour le marché de l’occasion. Il pourra néanmoins constituer une aide bienvenue pour les particuliers qui remplissent les conditions, mais son montant risque de rester largement symbolique face au prix d’une voiture électrique d’occasion. Pour le marché de l’occasion, le compte n’y est donc clairement pas encore.

articles.title: The Download: kids’ thoughts on AI, and female clones of male mice
articles.text:
The Download: kids’ thoughts on AI, and female clones of male mice
Plus: Trump has authorized businesses to conduct cyberattacks on criminals.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
How kids feel about AI, in their own words
—Jen Swetzoff and Keeley McNamara, the founding editors of Anyway, an independent print magazine for tweens and teens
When we set out to talk to kids about AI, we thought we knew what we’d hear. We expected stories about cheating, inspiring uses, and concerns like deepfakes or job destruction. But what we actually heard from kids aged 10 to 18 had tons of nuance.
Many were so deeply against AI or uninterested in making it part of their lives that they didn’t want to talk about it at all. Others worried about cheating, the environmental impact, or AI’s effect on creativity and critical thinking.
AI doesn’t yet seem to be something a lot of them are focused on—and they aren’t begging for it, the way they do for iPhones and Snapchat. But what surprised us most was how much young people could teach adults about AI.
Meet the kids navigating an AI-filled future—and hear what they think of it.
Scientists just created female clones of male mice
Scientists have deliberately turned male mouse embryos into females for the first time. A team based in Japan used a CRISPR-based approach to remove the Y chromosome from male cells and create female clones of male mice.
The feat could change the way scientists think about reproduction, says Takashi Ishiuchi, a reproductive biologist at the University of Yamanashi, who co-led the work. “There’s a fixed concept in our scientific field that we need both females and males for reproduction,” says Ishiuchi. “I think we could change this concept.”
He also hopes the technique could help rescue endangered species, particularly in cases where only a few individuals remain. Find out how it works—and what it could mean for the future of reproduction and conservation.
—Jessica Hamzelou
What’s behind this summer’s heat, and why 2027 could be worse
This summer has been a scorcher for much of the Northern Hemisphere. June and July marked the hottest two-month stretch in Europe since record-keeping began, the contiguous US endured its hottest month on record in July, and South Korea saw its highest-ever recorded temperature.
Climate change makes heat waves more likely and more intense. But there’s another factor at play: El Niño, which is already ramping up and is expected to have a bigger effect on global temperatures next year.
Here’s what’s behind this summer’s extreme heat—and why 2027 could be even hotter.
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Inside the "censorship-industrial complex" idea shaping US policy
For years, the idea of a “censorship-industrial complex” that suppressed conservative and populist speech spread in right-wing circles online. But now, the theory has made its way into the Trump administration.
Over the past nine months, MIT Technology Review investigated its origins and traced its rise.
In a virtual Roundtables session today, senior reporter Eileen Guo and executive editor Amy Nordrum will explore what they discovered, where the theory is going, and what it could mean for the future of democracy and the internet.
Register here to join the session at 19:00 GMT / 2:00 pm ET / 11:00 am PT.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Trump has authorized businesses to conduct cyberattacks on criminals
Vetted firms could use cyber tools against foreign criminal groups. (Reuters $)
+ They would operate under the control of the US government. (Bloomberg $)
+ Risks include escalation and inadvertent consequences. (Independent)
2 Chinese censorship is leaking into answers from American AI
ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini can all echo authoritarian propaganda. (WSJ $)
+ Turkey’s new cyber law has stoked fears of a digital police state. (FT $)
+ Censorship conspiracy theories have entered the US policy mainstream. (MIT Technology Review) 
3 Twitch is mining people’s streams to train Amazon’s AI
All streamers are opted in to train AI with their content by default. (404 Media)
+ Users can now opt out, but the announcement has sparked uproar. (BBC)
+ AI’s memories are privacy's next frontier. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Trump has been sued over a service selling faster access to his social posts
The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed the suit. (NPR)
+ They call the service “corrupt” and “unconstitutional.” (Ars Technica)
+ And say it violates the right of equal access to official information. (Reuters $)
5 Police officers are using Flock cameras to stalk people
Three Georgia deputies are the latest officers accused of abuse. (NYT $)
+ But the surveillance devices still have some supporters. (Atlantic $)
6 AI reporters are now breaking big news
One just beat human journalists to a story about hacking at OpenAI. (Wired $)
+ The milestone has sparked debate about the future of journalism. (Gizmodo)
7 The web’s newest weapon against AI scrapers is a font
ShieldFont foils scrapers but keeps pages readable to people. (Ars Technica)
8 Live streaming has turned us all into Perez Hilton
It’s made us both the celebrity and the paparazzi. (New Yorker $)
9 A fossil discovery suggests live birth emerged far earlier than thought
It pushes the origin of mammalian live birth back 95 million years. (New Scientist $)
10 Scientific progress may not be slowing after all
New research disputes claims that science is getting less disruptive. (Economist $)
Quote of the day
“Trump is trying to enrich himself by privatizing government information that he has no right to sell. We won’t let it stand.”
—Ben Muessig, editor-in-chief of The Intercept, explains why his media organization is suing President Trump over his fast-access service to Truth Social posts.
One More Thing
Puerto Rico’s power struggles
  Carmen Suárez Vázquez lives just minutes from Puerto Rico’s only coal-fired power plant. Black dust coats her windowpanes and the leaves of the blooming vines around her home. She doesn’t know exactly how the coal pollution got inside, but she is certain it ended up in her youngest son, Edgardo, who died of a rare form of cancer.
The plant was supposed to close in 2027. Instead, it will stay open for at least another seven years, while Puerto Rico rolls back clean-energy targets and moves ahead with new gas plants.
Meanwhile, residents are still dealing with frequent blackouts and high electricity prices. And an unelected fiscal control board has veto power over all spending by the island’s elected government, leaving Puerto Ricans with little say over their energy future.
Here’s why Puerto Rico can’t seem to escape its energy crisis.
— Alexander C. Kaufman
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ A double amputee has climbed the tallest mountain on every continent.
+ Enjoy a gorgeous coastal wander with Paul Theroux along the newly opened King Charles III England Coast Path.
+ A shrine for plush toys has opened in Kyoto, offering a place where visitors can pray with their favourite stuffed companions.
+ CrankGPT is a fully offline, off-the-grid AI box that makes a compelling argument that intelligent machines don’t need a data center. 
Deep Dive

Plus: OpenAI has unveiled its long-awaited "super app."

Plus: New York has become the first state to enact a data center moratorium.

Plus: Meta is pausing an AI training program that tracks workers’ keystrokes.
The Download: a reality check for geoengineering and the science of interoception
Plus: SpaceX is now valued higher than Amazon.

articles.title: Copper’s Grip On AI Scaling Is Starting To Slip
articles.text:
As AI clusters push beyond rack-scale limits, optical interconnects and circuit switching are reshaping how data centers scale.
Key Takeaways:
Data-center network fabrics are undergoing another architectural shift as optical interconnects assume a larger role in AI-cluster connectivity, extending into scale-up domains and influencing overall topology design.
Scale-up has typically been defined as a single rack with copper interconnect, with programmers using memory semantics. That definition is getting fuzzier.
“The old rule that scale-up is copper and scale-out is optical is starting to blur,” said Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus. “As data rates climb inside the rack, copper is running into physical limits around loss, reach, and power, challenging the ability of copper within a rack. From a signaling standpoint, optics can offer a cleaner scaling path at high data rates but must do so with manageable power and reliability over relatively short distances.”
Lower latency drives all of this, because GPUs underuse their capacity when they wait for data. “There have been a lot of reports on the efficiency of these GPUs that are maybe 25% efficient because they’re just sitting there waiting for data,” said Eric Aguilar, CEO and cofounder of Omnitron.
Google, meanwhile, implemented an optical circuit switching (OCS) network with a torus configuration, and others are also considering OCS networks for other network architectures.
This architectural shift also requires a more precise assessment of how scaling terminology is evolving across AI data-center networks.
Scaling evolves yet further
With an ever-shifting hierarchy of data-center scaling, particularly for AI workloads, this has rolled out as scale-up, scale-out, and scale-across approaches. 
More recently, scale-in has shown up. “This a new term that has only started in the last three months,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, head of product management at Ayar Labs. “It refers to the amount of bandwidth coming out of the GPU that stays within a single chassis.”
The definitions of these up until recently can be summed up as follows:
Aside from the addition of scale-in, scale-up is evolving. Computing clusters are growing beyond the bounds of a single rack, recruiting servers in adjacent racks. Now the interconnect distance is longer, and copper may no longer be the best medium. As a result, fiber is percolating into scale-up.
“If it’s going to be within a rack, you’re probably going to use copper,” explained Chandrasekar. “If it’s adjacent racks, you’re on the margin, but let’s say you stick with copper. If you’re going into anything more than adjacent racks, you’re going to go with optics.”
In terms of how long a link requires optics, “Assuming they’re using a 200-gig signaling rate, copper probably makes sense up to five or, if you really push it, seven meters,” Chandrasekar explained. “Certainly, once you hit 10 meters and beyond, it absolutely has to be optics.”
Scale-up as previously defined had three elements: single rack, copper, and memory semantics. The first two are now being phased out, and the remaining defining factor is the use of memory semantics.
“Software guys define scale-up as one operating system domain where they have one memory,” said Priyank Shukla, director of product management, interface IP at Synopsys. “So, if you’re running a process, the processor can write to one memory location, regardless of where that memory is.”
Typical implementations of scale-up and scale-out minimize the number of hops. “Within the scale-up domain, every GPU is just one hop away from every other GPU,” said Chandrasekar. “If you’re talking scale-out, it’s like two hops.”
The one-hop expectation for scale-up is enforced by the new UALink standard. “UALink scale-up fabrics are designed to maintain single-switch-hop accelerator-to-accelerator connectivity,” explained Shukla. “Even as a scale-up domain expands beyond a single rack, communication between accelerators is intended to traverse only a single UALink switch. As a result, connecting accelerators across racks does not inherently require a switch-to-switch topology that would introduce an additional hop. The single switch can be located in different places within the rack architecture, such as a Top of Rack (ToR) or Middle of Rack (MoR) deployment, but the key point is that accelerator traffic still traverses only one switch between endpoints.”
Once scale-up domains extend beyond the rack, the same latency and hop-count constraints shift attention from interconnect media to the broader network topology that links accelerators, switches, and servers.
Network architectures
The way servers are interconnected in the data center makes a power and performance difference, but there’s no single correct configuration. Different workloads benefit from different arrangements. 
One of the most common is called a Clos or leaf-and-spine network. Given two servers, there’s a short path between them. While this architecture is pervasive, one of the biggest players is using something else for its AI network.
“Google doesn’t have a leaf and spine network,” observed Chandrasekar. “It’s a torus network, which means every TPU is linked to adjacent TPUs, adjacent in three directions: up, down, and to the right, giving it a systolic character.”
Fig. 1: Network architectures. The top shows leaf-and-spine, with a one-hop path from any server to any server. Below is a torus, which requires more hops between any two servers. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
A key difference between the two is the number of hops necessary to get from any server to any other. With leaf-and-spine, it’s one. With torus, it depends on the locations. The path above shows four hops.
“If you want to get from one GPU on one end, to another GPU on the other end, you have lots of hops along the way,” Chandrasekar noted. A long-enough path can be implemented with optical for better power/performance. But each hop brings some inefficiency since the typical way these networks are built involves packet switching. Packets contain artifacts in their headers that must be inspected at each switch or router.
Optical technology doesn’t understand packets. So, the four-hop path above would require, at each hop, that the optical signal be converted to electrical. Once in the electrical domain, the next hop can be determined, but before the signal makes that next hop, it has to be converted back to optical.
These repeated conversions at each node hurt latency and consume a fair bit of energy. Is there a better way to build optical networks?
Circuit switching is old school
Packet switching is taken for granted today, but it’s not the original network. Previously, there were nationwide telephone systems that used circuit switches. Circuit switching means opening up an entire path from source to destination and giving exclusive use to one flow. In the old days, this flow was the conversation between the people at both ends of the line. Party lines aside, no one else could use that line while the conversation was busy. 
An analogy helps here. Let’s say you want to take a road trip from Los Angeles to Boston. In real life, you’d share the road with many other vehicles, and at each intersection or interchange, you and everyone else have an opportunity to change your route to get to your specific destination. Now, as anyone who has ever been held up by a traffic light knows, such travel would be so much easier if everyone else would go away and leave the road to you.
If you were to reserve the entire path from LA to Boston, eliminating all stops, you could get there much more quickly and efficiently. This is what a circuit-switched network provides. It comes with a slower background network that configures the path prior to enabling the conversation. For the phone system, the most recent of these is called Signaling System 7.
The problem is that even while you’re still in California, no one else can be on any of the other roads along the way, even right outside Boston. Only when you’d arrived would those roads be freed up for someone else’s trip, which sounds inefficient.
Packets to the rescue… for some things
This is where packet switching came in, which can be thought of as the stop signs, stop lights, and highway interchanges that allow multiple people to make multiple trips to completely different destinations all while using roads that others are also using. Replace those intersections with routers and the roads with wires, and you have the essence of a packet-switched network, which has become the standard for most of networking. 
What’s new is the data center challenge of repeated conversions between optical and electrical domains, due to packet routing. “Data moves by picking a fat, infinite-bandwidth fiber signal, putting it into an electrical switch, converting that optical signal to an electrical signal, reading the packet, and then routing it to another GPU,” explained Aguilar. “That optical-electrical-optical loop burns an enormous amount of power, adds latency, and drives up cost in data centers. About 15 years ago, Google started looking at this, and about 10 years ago, made it happen with a MEMS [microelectromechanical systems]-based optical circuit switch.”
The company uses nothing but adjustable MEMS mirrors at each router. Those mirrors reflect the laser light coming from the source fiber onto the destination fiber for that particular route. Those are set up at every node to provide a clear path from source to destination, with no conversions necessary. This approach is called optical circuit switching (OCS).
Google’s implementation
Google has found OCS beneficial. “We have spent the last eight years deeply integrating OCS and wave division multiplexing (WDM) into Jupiter [their network],” noted author Amin Vahdat, senior vice president and chief technologist, AI and Infrastructure at Google, in a paper from 2022. “The combination of OCS with our software-defined networking (SDN) architecture has enabled new capabilities: support for incremental network builds with heterogeneous technologies; higher performance and lower latency, cost, and power consumption; real-time application priority and communication patterns; and zero-downtime upgrades. Jupiter does all this while reducing flow completion by 10%, improving throughput by 30%, using 40% less power, incurring 30% less cost, and delivering 50× less downtime than the best-known alternatives.”
The power savings reflect a number of changes. “You’re eliminating half of the transceivers, eliminating the liquid cooling that’s required, and then the ASIC/electronics that are in the switch itself, and you’re replacing that with an optical solution,” said Aguilar.
In an OCS, when a large chunk of data must flow between two servers, first the background network configures the mirrors all along the route, then the flow can proceed with no conversions or routing decisions. The key here, however, is that this data all comes from the same place and goes to the same place. None of the data can branch off and travel to a different node. That makes this an optimization that’s workload-specific.
If this approach were taken for short, frequent bursts of data, more time would be spent setting up the routes and tearing them down than sending data. Using the road analogy, reserving the whole road from LA to Boston might make sense if there is a convoy that is longer than the full route. In that case, no one else can use the road while it’s occupied, but no part of it is sitting idle. This is similar to long data flows that warrant OCS.
“Optical circuit switching makes sense for ‘elephant flows,’ a term that I’ve been hearing others use,” said Aguilar. “It’s much better than these bursts of ‘mice flows.’ This is more for AI and large language-model learning and inferencing.”
And since OCS depends on reserving an end-to-end optical path before payload transmission begins, its effectiveness also depends on the control plane that configures those paths.
A new Signaling System
A background network configures the mirrors when the flow is set up. Analogous to Signaling System 7, it’s a slow Ethernet-based control network running alongside the optical network. “You have a lower-bandwidth Ethernet network to reconfigure the switches and the data route,” said Aguilar. 
It doesn’t take too long to reconfigure the network, but it does take time, which is another reason this makes sense only for long flows. Even so, configuring the network isn’t what limits how long a new configuration can be up and running. “It’s the transceiver lock that’s the bottleneck,” said Aguilar.
It may seem more complex to replace one network with two, but the control network isn’t complex. “You still have Ethernet that connects rack to rack to route the pipes to the right spots, but it’s a simpler, more elegant solution,” he said. It also doesn’t add significantly to capital costs. “Ethernet switches are cheap. The Ethernet switch is just a simple low-bandwidth command center.”
Mixing packet and circuit
The torus network in Figure 1 above uses point-to-point connections, and circuit switching benefits the many-hop connections. But the leaf/spine architecture is different: it features switches and routers. Could this architecture benefit from OCS as well? 
In the torus example, the flows are end-to-end. This could be done in a leaf/spine setup as well, although fewer hops mean less power savings. What some companies are reviewing is whether, for instance, the top tier of a leaf/spine network could be an OCS, with the source and destination routers accepting multiple packets on the input side, bundling them together for optical transport to the destination router, where the packets are extracted and finally sent, electrically, to their final nodes.
“OCS optical will terminate into a switch, and then after that, it’s electrical,” said Synopsys’ Shukla.
Fig. 2: Mixing circuit and packet switching. The top portion illustrates an end-to-end circuit in a tree-style network. If the optical path were limited to the router-to-router connection, then packets could be assembled in the source router and disassembled and rerouted electrically in the destination router. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
As long as the traffic is steady enough, with multiple packets from the source side targeting nodes connected to the final router, then it could make sense to open an optical path between the two switches. As shown in Figure 2, this may look somewhat trivial, but if the path between routers is complex and goes through many nodes, such a circuit could make sense.
Google’s OCS is a done deal, and in fact they’re moving from a torus network to yet another configuration called a dragonfly. Other companies have yet to deploy such a network, whether torus or some other tree-style option, but word on the street is that OCS is being considered by different companies for different networks.
“People are looking at that saying, ‘Can we use that technology in leaf and spine structures to replace the second layer with an OCS while keeping the first layer cloud packet switching?’” said Chandrasekar.
The initial switchover to optical is manageable. “There isn’t a significant overhaul in a data center to make this happen,” said Aguilar. “If I can retrofit my data centers with this solution, I reduce the power demand, or I can increase capacity in existing data centers.”
Once an optical network is in place, it doesn’t need further upgrades. The fiber has no idea what generation of transceiver or memory or processor is in use, so changing those generations doesn’t require changing the network.
This idea is still being mulled in the industry. “It’s more in the exploratory phase right now,” Chandrasekar added. “No one’s deployed it.”
Optical encroaches further
Both developments involve increasing optical participation in the data center. With scale-up, it’s now joining copper for the longest connections, making the complete set of scale-up connections a mix of copper and fiber. 
Optical standards will help. “The OCP is trying to define the standards so that everyone can play in the ecosystem,” said Aguilar. “Google has developed a lot of proprietary aspects, and it needs to be standardized in order for this to be adopted, or it won’t work right.”
If this takes off, will it stress optical suppliers with a sudden burst of demand? Aguilar doesn’t think so, based on planned production scaling and industry mergers. “For the next five years, based on our projections, we’re okay,” he said. “Our foundry partner is already scaling as a result of the expectation of growth, while Nvidia announced a $2 billion investment in Lumentum, and another $2 billion in Coherent for OCS.”
OCS, meanwhile, provides a way to make optical more efficient for long flows between two destinations, and gives data centers a new way to configure optical interconnect. “When you’re trying to do all these memory-latency-sensitive things, you want to reduce the number of hops, and being purely in the optical domain does help,” Aguilar noted.
Additionally, new alliances are forming. For instance, Lightmatter recently joined Nvidia’s NVLink ecosystem. But work remains.
“Many companies are currently evaluating this option, and from a technology point of view it makes a lot of sense,” said Ewald Liess, senior vice president of sales and business development at SignatureIP. “But with production costs and reliability, there are plenty of challenges to be solved.”
